newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Independent Gerling seeks foreign growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Independent Gerling seeks foreign growth.

text.p: German insurer Gerling said it was placing its faith in stronger foreign business and was determined to remain independent.
The family-owned company said however it would not necessarily object to its main outside shareholder Deutsche Bank AG taking a bigger stake.

Juergen Zech, chairman of the specialist in industrial cover, told reporters Wednesday evening that Gerling's fast-developing foreign business outstripped its domestic performance in the 1995/1996 business year.
"The group improved in virtually every area," Zech said.
Gerling, fully known as Gerling Konzern Versicherungs Beteiligungs AG, reported a slump in net earnings for the year ended June 30 1996 to 110 million marks ($69.3 million) from 274 million.

However the company stressed that its earnings from the previous period had been inflated by a one-off contribution from the sale in 1995 of its stake in reinsurance group Frankona Rueckversicherungs AG.
Gerling's premium income for 1995/1996 rose 6.5 percent to 11 billion marks, amid a 12.9 percent rise in international business, compared to more modest 3.7 percent growth at home.
Provisional figures showed premiums rose 7.5 percent in 1996 as a whole to 11.8 billion marks.
Looking ahead, Zech said Gerling was mainly aiming at internal growth but said he could not rule out the chance of acquisitions.

While Zech said Gerling was capable of financing its own growth plans for the next seven to ten years, he commented that the insurer would take a flexible view of Deutsche Bank taking a higher stake than its current 30 percent.
At the same time, the company 70 percent owned by the Gerling family was determined to remain independent so that Deutsche's stake would have to remain under 50 percent.
Zech also said company earnings this year would likely be hit by several large-ticket claims.
The freight train fire last November in the Channel Tunnel which injured 34 people is expected to cost Gerling, one of operator Eurotunnel's main insurers, around 120 million marks.

The total cost of the blaze, which closed the Channel Tunnel link for two weeks after causing serious damage to a section of the undersea passage, will be just under one billion marks, Zech estimated.
Among the other major claims it faces this year, Gerling said it expected a charge of around 50 million marks from a fire last April at the Duesseldorf airport.
While Gerling had not directly insured the airport, the charge for airline Deutsche Lufthsana's loss of business alone was more than 40 million marks.
Nonetheless, initial figures for the calendar year 1996 showed Gerling's claims ratio rose only slight to 71.5 percent from 71 percent.
